cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-sardis.summary: A bust of Christ with a cross-staff appears in a cloud-flecked sky at the upper left; below, John stands with a scroll, and an angel stands among the buildings of Sardis while a small group of figures gather and point.
facts: The Trier Apocalypse contains 74 full-page drawings illustrating about 150 episodes of the Book of Revelation; it is one of the earliest illustrated Apocalypse manuscripts to survive.
Its pictures are thought to copy a late antique model of the 4th–6th century, which explains features such as books shown as scrolls and Christ as the beardless Logos.
cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-sardis.notes: The Commons description assigns this page to the letter to Sardis; the exact letter illustrated is not certain.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-28-christ.summary: At the upper left the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos holding a book sits in a globe-mandorla among angels, and personified winds below him breathe out rays, the 'voice of the Lord' that is upon the waters, breaks the cedars of Lebanon and shakes the wilderness. On the right a procession of young men brings lambs to the sanctuary. The drawing gives visible form to a psalm about the sound of God's power.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-28-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects2-vam-anglo-saxon-pectoral-cr.summary: On this worn, oval pectoral of walrus ivory the crucified Christ stands calmly before the cross, his feet on a suppedaneum, while the Hand of God descends from a cloud above; four roundels around him hold the symbols of the Evangelists. A hollow cross-shaped cavity at the back once held a relic, so that the wearer carried both the image and the relic of Christ's Passion close to the heart.
facts: The V&A links the figure style and the Hand of God to late Anglo-Saxon stone roods such as those at Stepney and Romsey.
Such pectoral crosses, worn on a chain or cord, were commonly worn by bishops and abbots.
The cross is only 9 cm high.
